# Rockets and spaceflight (`rocket_spaceflight`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by laws_of_motion, universal_gravitation, war_rockets
- Core idea: A rocket is pushed by the reaction of the gas it throws backwards and needs no air, so it works in space. The speed gained equals the exhaust speed times the natural logarithm of the ratio of full to empty mass (Tsiolkovsky), so reaching orbit (about 7.8 km/s sideways, beyond the air) needs high exhaust speeds (liquid fuels such as kerosene or hydrogen with liquid oxygen), multiple stages that drop their empty tanks, and guidance. An orbiting craft is falling around the Earth all the time, like Newton's cannonball.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying a rocket needs air to push against
  - Thinking getting to space means going high; orbit is about speed sideways
  - Ignoring re-entry heating; returning craft need heat shields
- History: china: 13th c. – gunpowder rockets ('fire arrows') in Song and Jin warfare (the date of the first true rocket is disputed); india: 1780s–1790s – iron-cased Mysore rockets of Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan, which inspired Congreve's; europe: 1903 – Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation; 1923 Oberth; 1944 the V-2 is the first object to reach space; 1957 Sputnik; 1961 Gagarin; americas: 16 March 1926 – Goddard's liquid-fuel rocket; 1969 Apollo 11 lands on the Moon
- Read:
  - Robert H. Goddard, A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes (1919)
  - Walter A. McDougall, ...the Heavens and the Earth: A Political History of the Space Age (1985)
